messages.subject: WG: NIMBLE version 1.0.0 released, providing automatic differentiation, Laplace approximation, and HMC sampling
messages.subject_clean: WG: NIMBLE version 1.0.0 released, providing automatic differentiation, Laplace approximation, and HMC sampling
messages.body_plain:
NIMBLE development is going on and on and on …. 😊

Von: nimble...@googlegroups.com <nimble...@googlegroups.com> Im Auftrag von Chris Paciorek
Gesendet: Donnerstag, 1. Juni 2023 13:41
An: nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com>; nimble-...@googlegroups.com
Betreff: NIMBLE version 1.0.0 released, providing automatic differentiation, Laplace approximation, and HMC sampling

We're very pleased to announce the release of version 1.0.0 of NIMBLE. This version provides substantial new functionality. This includes:

A Laplace approximation algorithm that allows one to find the MLE for model parameters based on approximating the marginal likelihood in models with continuous random effects/latent process values.
A Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) MCMC sampler implementing the NUTS algorithm (available in the newly-released `nimbleHMC` package).
Support in NIMBLE's algorithm programming system to obtain derivatives of functions and arbitrary calculations within models.
A parameter transformation system allowing algorithms to work in unconstrained parameter spaces when model parameters have constrained domains.

These are documented via the R help system and a new section at the end of our User Manual <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-AD.html>. We’re excited for users to try out the new features and let us know of their experiences. In particular, given these major additions to the NIMBLE system, we anticipate the possibility of minor glitches. The best place to reach out for support is still the nimble-users list <https://r-nimble.org/more/issues-and-groups>.

In addition to the new functionality above, other enhancements and bug fixes include:

Fixing a bug (previously reported in a nimble-users message) giving incorrect results in NIMBLE’s cross-validation function (`runCrossValidate`) for all but the ‘predictive’ loss function for NIMBLE versions 0.10.0 - 0.13.2.
Fixing a bug in conjugacy checking causing incorrect identification of conjugate relationships in models with unusual uses of subsets, supersets, and slices of multivariate normal nodes.
Improving control of the `addSampler` method for MCMC.
Improving the WAIC system in a few small ways.
Enhancing error trapping and warning messages.

Please see the  NEWS file <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/nimble/inst/NEWS.md> in the package source for more details.

- Chris Paciorek for the NIMBLE Development Team

--

messages.subject: Info on site replacement in occupancy models
messages.subject_clean: Info on site replacement in occupancy models
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am a Ph.D. student at the University of Pisa (Italy).
I have a systematic grid of camera traps active through all the year, and I check them periodically to retrieve the data and change batteries. Unfortunately, sometimes a camera may be stolen (let's name it camera 1), and in that case I replace the camera but, for obvious reasons, I move it to another spot (camera 2). Specifically, I search for a suitable site within approx. 300m on the same trail, but if I don't find a site safe enough (the study area poses a lot of constraints) I move it to a nearby wildlife trail within the same distance.
I plan to use multi-season occupancy models for these data, and my question is: do you believe I could consider the two sites (camera 1 and 2) as the same, since they are not simultaneously active and represent the same sampling unit? Or should I consider them as separate units and build up detection histories (and covariates) for each one separately (for example, camera 1 active in season 1, NAs for season 2; and the opposite for camera 2)?
And, in the second case, which is the most convenient (or effective) approach to handle the plausible autocorrelation between the two sites (sites closer to each other should be more autocorrelated respect to all the other more or less equally-spaced sites in the grid)?

Best regards,

Luca

messages.subject: AW: Info on site replacement in occupancy models
messages.subject_clean: AW: Info on site replacement in occupancy models
messages.body_plain:
Dear Luca

the answer to these questions may depend on the spacing of the cameras in general, the distance between the original site of a camera and the replacement site, and the size of the activity range of your study species. If camera trap spacing or inter-site distance is small relative to the activity range size, then you could probably just ignore the change and assign old and replacement camera site to the same “site” in the occupancy model.

On the other hand, you could also treat them as two sites and fill up the data with missing values, as you describe. Actually, you hardly lose much information if you do this: in the case of a dynamic occupancy model, you may lose the information towards the estimation of a single transition (i.e., colonization and extinction/persistence parameter).

About spatial autocorrelation: from what you described to me about your design off-list, I don’t think you have enough data to do any spatial autocorrelation modeling.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Doctor Kéry,

Thanks for your answer.
I am specifically referring to the wolf as the target species, and the distance between camere 1 and camera 2 is generally lower than 500m, thus way smaller than the average home range of wolves (only in a case it is about 900m; this was due to multiple thefts). Furthermore, I am only interested in estimating occupancy and its trend over the years (with a static multi-season approach).
Regarding spatial autocorrelation, in this case I am not referring to the dataset I told you about off-list, whereas this is a systematic dataset of 40-50 camera traps. Anyway, I am trying not to overcomplicate the model, and I was thinking about including a random site effect with common mean for sites within a certain distance from each other; do you believe this could help in controlling for autocorrelation?

Best regards,

Luca

messages.subject: Re: spreadsheet data format
messages.subject_clean: spreadsheet data format
messages.body_plain:
Dear Joaquin,

there are many different possible formats to put your data into. I'd put them in a site by (year & visit) format, as shown in the attached file for a simulated toy data set with 4 sites, 2 years and a maximum of 4 visits per site. This is the format required for the colext() function in unmarked and it's also easy to work with it when using a general model-fitting engine such as JAGS or NIMBLE (although there I'd then put the detection/nondetection data into a 3D array with dimensions site x visit x year).

Best regards  --- Marc

Dear Luca,

about spatial autocorrelation: what you suggest, with overlapping spatial strata for which you estimate a shared random effect, does not sound bad to me, but I have never seen such overlapping strata being estimated (except for the CAR model, which does do this in a sense). But you could try out functions in the R package spOccupancy. There you could also use WAIC for comparing a spatial with a non-spatial model.

Best regards  -- Marc

Anyway, I am trying not to overcomplicate the model, and I was thinking about including a random site effect with common mean for sites within a certain distance from each other; do you believe this could help in controlling for autocorrelation?

Best regards,

Luca

>
>
> the answer to these questions may depend on the spacing of the cameras in general, the distance between the original site of a camera and the replacement site, and the size of the activity range of your study species. If camera trap spacing or inter-site distance is small relative to the activity range size, then you could probably just ignore the change and assign old and replacement camera site to the same “site” in the occupancy model.
>
>
>
> On the other hand, you could also treat them as two sites and fill up the data with missing values, as you describe. Actually, you hardly lose much information if you do this: in the case of a dynamic occupancy model, you may lose the information towards the estimation of a single transition (i.e., colonization and extinction/persistence parameter).
>
>
>
> About spatial autocorrelation: from what you described to me about your design off-list, I don’t think you have enough data to do any spatial autocorrelation modeling.
>
>
>
> Best regards  --- Marc

>

> I have a systematic grid of camera traps active through all the year, and I check them periodically to retrieve the data and change batteries. Unfortunately, sometimes a camera may be stolen (let's name it camera 1), and in that case I replace the camera but, for obvious reasons, I move it to another spot (camera 2). Specifically, I search for a suitable site within approx. 300m on the same trail, but if I don't find a site safe enough (the study area poses a lot of constraints) I move it to a nearby wildlife trail within the same distance.
>
> I plan to use multi-season occupancy models for these data, and my question is: do you believe I could consider the two sites (camera 1 and 2) as the same, since they are not simultaneously active and represent the same sampling unit? Or should I consider them as separate units and build up detection histories (and covariates) for each one separately (for example, camera 1 active in season 1, NAs for season 2; and the opposite for camera 2)?

messages.subject: Occupancy GOF discrepancy between Bayesian and Frequentist
messages.subject_clean: Occupancy GOF discrepancy between Bayesian and Frequentist
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am running a single-season single-species Bayesian occupancy model on systematic camera trapping data calling JAGS from jagsUI in R.
I planned of testing GOF by using the code for the "closed part of the model" from chapter 4.8.2 in AHM2 (Kery and Royle, 2021). Basically, it is a calculation of both a Chi-squared and a Freeman-Tukey discrepancy stats.
The problem is, I obtain a very bad fit and overdispersion for the NULL MODEL, despite having a quite robust dataset (33 sites simultaneously active for 3 months, naive occupancy approx. 0.6). Furthermore, and this is the strangest part, if I try fitting the same null model in unmarked, both the MacKenzie-Bailey test and the same Chi-squared and FT statistics (code from Andrade-Ponce et al. 2022) result in a good fit and no overdispersion at all.
Is there a plausible reason why I obtain such different results in GOF testing between Bayesian and Frequentist methods? Am I missing something?

Thank you in advance.

Luca

messages.subject: Re: Occupancy GOF discrepancy between Bayesian and Frequentist
messages.subject_clean: Occupancy GOF discrepancy between Bayesian and Frequentist
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dr. Hollanders,

here is the code, almost the same as in the book.

# Draw a replicate data set under the fitted model
for (i in 1:nsites){
    for (j in 1:nsurveys){
      yrep[i,j] ~ dbern(z[i] * p)
  }
}

# Compute detection frequencies for observed and replicated data
for (i in 1:nsites){
    # Det. frequencies for observed and replicated data
    detfreq[i] <- sum(y[i,])
    detfreqrep[i] <- sum(yrep[i,])
    # Expected detection frequencies under the model
    for (j in 1:nsurveys){
      tmp[i,j] <- z[i] * p
    }
    E[i] <- sum(tmp[i,])     # Expected number of detections
    # Chi-square and Freeman-Tukey discrepancy measures
    # ..... for actual data set
    x2[i] <- pow((detfreq[i] - E[i]),2) / (E[i]+0.00000001)
    ft[i] <- pow((sqrt(detfreq[i]) - sqrt(E[i])),2)
    # ..... for replicated data set
    x2rep[i] <- pow((detfreqrep[i] - E[i]),2) / (E[i]+0.00000001)
    ftrep[i] <- pow((sqrt(detfreqrep[i]) - sqrt(E[i])),2)
  }

# Add up Chi-square and FT discrepancies and compute fit stat ratio (closed part)
Chi2 <- sum(x2)
FT <- sum(ft)
Chi2rep <- sum(x2rep)
FTrep <- sum(ftrep)
Chi2.chat <- Chi2 / Chi2rep
FT.chat <- FT / FTrep
Chi2.bpv <- step(Chi2rep-Chi2)
FT.bpv <- step(Chi2rep-Chi2)

Thanks for your response,

Luca

messages.subject: Single-Season Model for Real-Time Estimates of HABs
messages.subject_clean: Single-Season Model for Real-Time Estimates of HABs
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm interested in using a single-season model to estimate daily occurrence probabilities of harmful algal blooms (HABs). Because HAB longevity can be quite short (i.e., 24-48 hrs) my inclination is to use spatial replicates to generate the necessary detection histories. By using this design, a site would be sampled in a single day, thus ensuring each site was closed to changes in occupancy during the defined sampling season. The use of this sampling design would be novel because it would allow scientists to get a much better sense of what environmental gradients serve as primary triggers of HAB development in aquatic systems at an important time-step (daily) while also controlling for the influence of detection.

Anyways, I wanted to see if anyone on the HM group could identify any major red flags in the described design that were in my blind spot.

Sincerely,

Josh

messages.subject: Multi-state CJS with long term data
messages.subject_clean: Multi-state CJS with long term data
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I am working on a two decade long data set of capture recapture data, trying to get a multi-state CJS model to look at age structure (juvenile and adults) and body condition within adults. The population is an island, so it is closed to immigration, but there is reproduction and death over the study period.

I've tried a few different formulations, including with and without a "not entered" state, but I can never get the model to mix well. Running the models with Nimble I get warning messages of -Inf log probability for some nodes, and some values of estimates for survival and transition probabilities dont mix at all (zero variance in posterior).

I'm not sure if the issue is model formulation or initial values, or a combination of both. If anyone has an idea of some similar sort of examples that I could explore to help me out that'd be great. I've also attached an R script of two versions of the model I've tried. Thanks in advance.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: AW: Multi-state CJS with long term data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

One problem with your model is that the transition matrix is not row stochastic, i.e. not all rows sum to 1. The sum to one is necessary because individuals must make a state transition between t and t+1 with probability 1.

Otherwise, the model looks good and should work.

Kind regards

Michael

Dear all,

We have a funded 2-year postdoc position in quantitative ecology available at SEEC (The Centre for Statistics in Ecology, Environment and Conservation) at the University of Cape Town in South Africa. The postdoc will be responsible for the development of capture-recapture and integrated population models to assess the efficacy of conservation measures for African penguins. The project is in collaboration with SANCCOB (the Southern African Foundation for the Conservation of Coastal Birds) and the University of Exeter.

Please see full details in the attached pdf or  this link <https://drive.google.com/file/d/15ophZpMs3IzDK8bzcMxtejhHnTrFWowl/view?usp=sharing>.  Application deadline is 21 July. Please feel free to share this announcement with your colleagues or on your platforms.
